title: Describing things
job: Size, colour, quality — agreement at length
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A plural of NON-HUMAN things takes a FEMININE SINGULAR adjective: al-kutub jamīla — "the books, she is beautiful". Only a plural of people takes a plural adjective: al-mudarrisūn mashghūlūn. English has no such split, so "plural noun, plural adjective" is wrong in Arabic more often than it is right.

One al- decides whether three words are a phrase or a sentence. al-bayt al-kabīr is "the big house"; al-bayt kabīr is "the house is big". An attributive adjective matches its noun in definiteness; a predicate does not, and the mismatch IS the verb.

Three plural systems and none of them is predictable: sound masculine -ūn on human nouns, sound feminine -āt, and BROKEN plurals that reshape the word from inside — kitāb → kutub, bayt → buyūt, walad → awlād, lawn → alwān.
Colours follow their own pattern: aḥmar for a masculine thing and ḥamrāʾ for a feminine one. The feminine is NOT the -a you have been writing since the first module, so the pair is learnt together.
A broken plural belongs in the forms of the row that teaches its singular, and no rule in this course claims the shape can be worked out. It cannot.

words.note: Carries al- because al-bayt does — an attributive adjective matches its noun in definiteness. kabīr does not, and that is what makes it the predicate.

sentences.trap: Two adjectives, one with al- and one without, and the al- is what tells them apart. Give kabīr an al- as well and the sentence loses its verb and becomes a phrase.
sentences.sound: al-BAYT al-ja-DĪD ka-BĪR — three stresses, and the al- of the second word is barely voiced.

variations.changed: the two adjectives swap jobs, and only the al- moves
both take al-, so there is no sentence left — only a phrase
no al- anywhere, so it is an indefinite phrase

mistake.why: That is a phrase, not a sentence — "the big new house". The predicate must go without al-: al-bayt al-jadīd kabīr.

sentences.usage: The single most useful pattern in the level: it is how Arabic says "is" without a verb.
sentences.mnemonic: The word without al- is the one doing the saying.

words.note: Feminine SINGULAR, because al-kutub are things and not people. Arabic treats a non-human plural as one feminine thing. The row for jamīl is M9's from the level below.

sentences.trap: The books are plural and the adjective is singular. Every instinct an English speaker has says jamīlāt, and it is wrong here.
sentences.sound: al-KU-tub ja-MĪ-la — and the -a of jamīla is short, not the long ā of the plural.

variations.changed: another non-human plural, another feminine singular
an attributive adjective, also feminine singular, also with al-
one book, and the adjective goes masculine singular

mistake.why: Books are not people. A non-human plural takes a feminine singular adjective: al-kutub jamīla.

sentences.usage: Everywhere. This law governs every plural sentence in the rest of the course.
sentences.mnemonic: Things in a heap are one feminine thing.

sentences.cue: The cars are big and beautiful

words.note: The al-'d shape of M8's sayyārāt, and its own key: s is a sun letter, so the article assimilates and the build sees a different word from al-sayyārāt.
The same feminine singular as jamīla, and for the same reason: cars are things. The row for kabīr is L1-M3's.

sentences.trap: Both adjectives go feminine singular, not just the first. The rule governs every adjective in the sentence.
sentences.sound: as-say-yā-RĀT, with the y doubled and held, and the al- swallowed into the s.

variations.changed: one adjective, same shape

variations.cue: The car is big and beautiful
variations.changed: one car — and the adjectives do not change at all
an attributive adjective with al-, and a predicate without

mistake.why: Cars are things: as-sayyārāt kabīra. The -āt plural on the noun says nothing about the adjective.

sentences.usage: Notice what the second variation shows: one car and many cars take the SAME adjective. That is the law being useful rather than merely odd.
sentences.mnemonic: One car or twenty, the adjective does not move.

words.note: The sound masculine plural: -ūn on a human noun. It is the one plural in Arabic you can build rather than learn, and only people take it.
A plural adjective, because the teachers are PEOPLE. This is the other half of M3's law, and the row for mashghūl is M6's from the level below.

sentences.trap: This is the sentence that makes the law usable. Books take a feminine singular; teachers take a plural. What decides is whether the plural is human.
sentences.sound: mu-dar-ri-SŪN, mash-ghū-LŪN — both stressed on the long ū of the ending.

variations.changed: another plural adjective about people
one teacher, and both words go singular

variations.cue: The books are beautiful and the teachers are kind
variations.changed: both halves of the law in one sentence

mistake.why: Teachers are people, so the adjective goes plural: mashghūlūn. The feminine singular is only for things.

sentences.usage: Any sentence about a group of people. The last variation is the one to reread — it holds both rules side by side.
sentences.mnemonic: People take a plural; everything else takes a she.

words.note: Colours have their own shape: aḥmar for a masculine thing, ḥamrāʾ for a feminine one. Word-initial hamza is not written, so it starts with a plain a.

sentences.trap: aḥmar looks like the comparative shape M9 will teach — akbar, arkhaṣ — and it is not a comparison at all. The pattern is shared; the root decides the meaning.
sentences.sound: AḤ-mar, with the ḥ a hard breath and the stress at the front.

variations.changed: one adjective instead of two
the colour takes al- and becomes the description
indefinite, with M2's ʿindī

mistake.why: With al- on all three it is a phrase — "the big red house" — and there is no sentence left.

sentences.usage: Neutral description. The definiteness rule from S01 is doing all the work here.
sentences.mnemonic: The colour pattern and the comparative pattern are the same shape, and only the root knows which.

words.note: The feminine of aḥmar, and it is nothing like the -a ending every other adjective takes. The final hamza is written ʾ, and dropping it makes a different word.

sentences.trap: ḥamrāʾ, not aḥmara. The colour pattern has its own feminine and it must be learnt with the masculine, as a pair.
sentences.sound: ḥam-RĀʾ, ending in a clean catch of the throat after the long ā.

variations.changed: one adjective, and the sentence is three words shorter
a non-human plural, which takes the same feminine singular
indefinite, with M2's ʿindahā

mistake.why: There is no aḥmara. The feminine of aḥmar is ḥamrāʾ, a different shape entirely.

sentences.usage: The second variation is worth pausing on: the same word covers one car and many, because cars are things.
sentences.mnemonic: Colours keep their own feminine, and it is not an -a.

sentences.cue: The book is blue and the door is black

words.note: The same pattern as aḥmar, with the feminine zarqāʾ. The q is made at the back of the throat, well behind an English k.
The feminine is sawdāʾ. Three colours in this module, three identical patterns, and the feminine is never predictable from the -a rule.
The al-'d shape of M7's bāb, and its own key — b is a moon letter, so the l is written and said.

sentences.trap: wa is written joined to the word after it — والباب — but it is a free word in the romanized line. The two lines disagree about where a word ends, and that is on purpose.
sentences.sound: AZ-raq, AS-wad — both stressed at the front, like aḥmar.

variations.changed: the second half alone
the feminine of azraq
a non-human plural, and the feminine singular again

mistake.why: The article keeps its hyphen in the romanization: al-bāb. Running it into the noun would give the index a word nobody meant.

sentences.usage: Two clauses, no verb in either, joined by one letter. Arabic gets a lot said with very little.
sentences.mnemonic: wa joins in the script and stands alone in the reading.

words.note: A BROKEN plural of bayt: the word is reshaped from inside rather than given an ending. kitāb → kutub does the same. No rule predicts the shape, so it is learnt with the singular.

sentences.trap: There is no ending to add and no ending to look for. A broken plural rebuilds the word around the same three consonants.
sentences.sound: bu-YŪT, and the y is a full consonant between the two vowels.

variations.changed: the feminine singular adjective, because houses are things
another broken plural, from M8 of the level below

variations.cue: The houses in Egypt are big
variations.changed: definite, with the predicate after the place

mistake.why: bayt has a broken plural, buyūt. The -āt ending belongs to other words and cannot be added at will.

sentences.usage: The plural a learner will meet first, and the one that shows why Arabic plurals are learnt one at a time.
sentences.mnemonic: Broken plurals are rebuilt, not extended.

words.note: A broken plural of walad, and it is HUMAN — so the adjective goes plural, not feminine singular. A mixed group of children takes the masculine.
The sound masculine plural of M2's laṭīf, on an adjective this time. The row for laṭīf is L2-M2's.

sentences.trap: A BROKEN plural can still be human. It is not the shape of the plural that decides the adjective, it is what the noun refers to.
sentences.sound: al-aw-LĀD, with the aw as in English "how" and the stress on the long ā.

variations.changed: another plural adjective about people

variations.cue: The children are kind and busy
variations.changed: two plural adjectives, both about people
indefinite, with no al- anywhere

mistake.why: Children are people, so the adjective goes plural: laṭīfūn. Being a broken plural changes nothing.

sentences.usage: The sentence that separates the two halves of the law properly: the plural's shape and the plural's humanity are different questions.
sentences.mnemonic: Ask what it IS, not what shape its plural takes.

words.note: The broken plural of lawn. Its singular has not been shown in a sentence, so the row carries both — the one place in this module where the plural arrives first.

sentences.trap: Three words, and every one of the module's rules is in it: the broken plural, the definiteness match on al-jadīda, and the feminine singular predicate on jamīla.
sentences.sound: al-al-WĀN, and the two al sounds are different — the first is the article, the second is part of the word.

variations.changed: without the attributive adjective in the middle
the singular, and the l of al- doubling into the l of lawn
a colour as the predicate, still feminine singular

mistake.why: Colours are things: jamīla. A whole module of the rule, and it is the last sentence that tests whether it stuck.

sentences.usage: The module's summary in three words. If this one is right, the law is learnt.
sentences.mnemonic: Every rule of the module, in three words.
